extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in political theory, public opinion, and democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: A close analytic account of how majorities can exert oppressive power (legally or socially) and of the related psychological tendency—the 'fatalism of the multitude'—that disposes individuals to acquiesce. The text identifies causes, historical examples, and conditions that increase or reduce these dangers in democratic societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative oppressiveness (tyranny by law)
rubrics_metrics.description: If laws of general application operate to the injury of any class, instances of tyranny by law should appear; such enactments are the clearest form of majority tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that in the United States such general oppressive laws are not found; some provisions regulating corporations, railroads, and banks may be unwise and limit modes of using capital (affecting the rich rather than the masses) but are not properly 'wanton or oppressive.' Use presence of broadly harmful, class-targeting statutes as an indicator of legal tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: State statutes and constitutional safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions containing guarantees for free speech, a free press, and public meeting limit the capacity of state statutes to repress opinion or encroach on personal liberty and private property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where constitutional fundamentals exist and are respected, the legislature is less able to trample minority rights; evaluation of state-level tyranny should check for such constitutional protections and their practical enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of legislative interference in minor matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a law is a legitimate exercise of legislative authority in 'minor matters' (e.g. sale of intoxicants, education taxation, moral legislation) is contested and depends on differing moral and political views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists contested examples—prohibition of intoxicants, taxation to support public or denominational schools, restrictions on property use—and emphasizes that perceptions of 'tyranny' vary by viewpoint; when assessing legislative measures in these domains, account for plural moral perspectives and avoid conflating disagreement with tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social penalties and informal persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: A majority may tyrannize not only by law but by imposing social penalties—disapproval, insult, injury, boycotting—which can coerce conformity without legal enactment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure social persecution by prevalence and severity of ostracism, boycotts, or social sanctions; the author observes such persecution is rare in America overall but may exist in 'dark corners' or small communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical indicators of majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative persecution, mob violence, and social terror against dissenters (e.g. persecution of abolitionists, punitive laws in Slave States, local statutes enforcing orthodoxy) are historical signs of majority tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical examples—legislative and extra-legal violence (Prudence Crandall's persecution, mobs attacking Garrison, Lovejoy's murder, killing of Joseph Smith, reign of terror in the South)—as concrete evidence that majorities once exercised oppressive power; compare past and present occurrence to evaluate change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of violent passions as a reducing factor
rubrics_metrics.description: When violent passions or existential crises (e.g. slavery, disunion) are absent, majorities are less tempted to abuse legal powers; national trials (e.g. Civil War) can teach sobriety and reduce tendencies toward tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether intense, existential political passions are present; their absence, along with maturing political institutions, predicts lower risk of legal tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural expansion and separation of religion from politics promote tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended culture, popularized education, and the disjunction of religious and political questions reduce bigotry and make repression of speculative thought less likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for widespread education, openness to external intellectual influences, and institutional separation of church and state as protective conditions against majority intolerance; the author treats these as durable safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatalism of the multitude (individual acquiescence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In very large, socially and politically equal democracies individuals may feel themselves insignificant—a 'fatalistic' attitude that disposes them to acquiesce in the rule of numbers even without coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify structural features (scale of polity, equal political weight of all, social levelling) that produce a sense that 'one man's voice' cannot change the outcome; use indicators of individual resignation, diminished sense of personal responsibility, and lowered will to resist as measures of fatalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief that the majority is right (normative presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-government contains an implicit presumption that the majority must prevail and is likely right; repeated electoral success strengthens this presumption and weakens minority resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the extent to which political culture equates majority decisions with correctness—look for deference to electoral outcomes, demoralization of defeated minorities, and the psychological effect of successive victories that render second battles harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of discussion can produce acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussion is free and every view has been heard, those whom the multitude condemns or ignores have no further court of appeal and may accept judgment—so openness can paradoxically contribute to fatalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between repressive regimes (where denial of voice foments resistance) and free-regime dynamics (where being heard and then outvoted may foster submission); use presence of genuinely open forums plus subsequent acquiescence as a sign that fatalism, not coercion, is at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: National faith and optimism as causes of submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Intense faith in national institutions, a collective mission, and optimistic confidence that 'things will come out right' predispose citizens to accept majority decisions and to assume long-term correctness of social outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess civic religion, public optimism about institutions, and belief in national destiny as cultural factors that encourage submission rather than resistance; note the author's examples of religious conviction and pride in the Republic as contributing to acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between fatalism and coercive tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Fatalism (internalized resignation) differs from the tyranny of the majority (external legal or social coercion); fatalism softens or dispenses with overt exercise of power by inducing voluntary conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating threats to liberty, separate internal psychological capitulation (fatalism) from active coercion; both harm pluralism but require different remedies—restoring avenues of effective influence vs. curbing coercive institutions.
